text: Start by saying what the statement is that you want to prove: "Let \(P(n)\) be the statement..." To prove that \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n \ge 0\), you must prove two facts: (1) Base case: Prove that \(P(0)\) is true. You do this directly. This is often easy. (2) Inductive case: Prove that \(P(k) \rightarrow P(k+1)\) for all \(k \ge 0\). That is, prove that for any \(k \ge 0\) if \(P(k)\) is true, then \(P(k+1)\) is true as well. This is the proof of an if ... then ... statement, so you can assume \(P(k)\) is true (\(P(k)\) is called the inductive hypothesis). You must then explain why \(P(k+1)\) is also true, given that assumption. Assuming you are successful on both parts above, you can conclude, "Therefore by the principle of mathematical induction, the statement \(P(n)\) is true for all \(n \ge 0\)."
title: Induction Proof Structure

text: (1) An \(n\)-bit string is a bit string of length \(n\). That is, it is a string containing \(n\) symbols, each of which is a bit, either 0 or 1. (2) The weight of a bit string is the number of 1's in it. (3) \(\B^n\) \(\B^n\) the set of length \(n\) bit strings is the set of all \(n\)-bit strings. (4) \(\B^n_k\) \(\B^n_k\) the set of length \(n\) bit strings with weight \(k\). is the set of all \(n\)-bit strings of weight \(k\).

text: Suppose \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) and \(c \equiv d \pmod{n}\). Then the following hold: (1) \(a+c \equiv b+d \pmod{n}\). (2) \(a-c \equiv b-d \pmod{n}\). (3) \(ac \equiv bd \pmod{n}\).

text: For each integer \(n \ge 0\) and integer \(k\) with \(0 \le k \le n\) there is a number \[{n\choose k}\], read "\(n\) choose \(k\)." We have: (1) \({n\choose k} = |\B^n_k|\), the number of \(n\)-bit strings of weight \(k\). (2) \({n \choose k}\) is the number of subsets of a set of size \(n\) each with cardinality \(k\). (3) \({n \choose k}\) is the number of lattice paths of length \(n\) containing \(k\) steps to the right. (4) \({n \choose k}\) is the coefficient of \(x^ky^{n-k}\) in the expansion of \((x+y)^n\). (5) \({n \choose k}\) is the number of ways to select \(k\) objects from a total of \(n\) objects.

text: \(P \iff Q\) is logically equivalent to \((P \rightarrow Q) \wedge (Q \rightarrow P)\). Example: Given an integer \(n\), it is true that \(n\) is even if and only if \(n^2\) is even. That is, if \(n\) is even, then \(n^2\) is even, as well as the converse: if \(n^2\) is even, then \(n\) is even.

text: Given any integers \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\), and any positive integer \(n\), the following hold: (1) \(a \equiv a \pmod{n}\). (2) If \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) then \(b \equiv a \pmod{n}\). (3) If \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) and \(b \equiv c \pmod{n}\), then \(a \equiv c \pmod{n}\). In other words, congruence modulo \(n\) is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, so is an equivalence relation.
title: Congruence Modulo n is an Equivalence Relation
